title: Musculoskeletal, Rheumatology and Dermatology
summary: Joints, autoimmune disease and the skin.

lessons.title: Approach to Joint Pain

levels.kid:
Joints are the places where bones meet, like your knees, elbows and fingers. They let you bend and move.

Joints can hurt for two main reasons. Sometimes they are **worn out or hurt**, like a door hinge that has been used a lot. That kind of pain gets worse when you use the joint.

Other times the joint is **inflamed**, which means the body's defenders are making it swollen, warm and stiff. That kind is often stiff in the morning and feels better after you move around.

If one joint suddenly becomes red, hot, swollen and very painful, and you have a fever, a doctor must check it fast, because germs might be inside.
levels.hs:
Joint pain (**arthralgia**) is very common. When a joint is actually swollen or inflamed, it is called **arthritis**. Doctors sort joint problems with a few key questions.

**Inflammatory or mechanical?**
- **Inflammatory** pain: morning stiffness lasting more than about 30 to 60 minutes, warmth, swelling, and pain that **improves with movement**. Examples: rheumatoid arthritis, gout, infection.
- **Mechanical** pain: brief morning stiffness, pain that **worsens with use** and eases with rest. Example: osteoarthritis, the "wear and tear" arthritis.

**How many joints?**
- **One joint (monoarthritis):** infection, gout, injury.
- **Two to four (oligoarthritis):** reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis.
- **Five or more (polyarthritis):** rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, viral arthritis.

**Which joints?** Rheumatoid arthritis affects the knuckles and wrists on both sides. Osteoarthritis hits knees, hips, and the finger joints nearest the nails. Gout loves the big toe.

**The golden rule:** a single hot, swollen joint is an **infection until proven otherwise**. Doctors put a needle into the joint to draw fluid (**aspiration**) and test it for bacteria and crystals. An infected joint can be destroyed within days.

Doctors also look outside the joints: skin rashes, eye inflammation, mouth ulcers and back pain can all point to the cause.
levels.college:
A structured joint history covers onset, pattern, distribution, inflammatory features and extra-articular clues.

**Distribution patterns:**
- **Rheumatoid arthritis:** symmetric small joints (MCPs, PIPs, wrists, MTPs), **sparing the DIPs**.
- **Osteoarthritis:** DIPs (**Heberden nodes**), PIPs (**Bouchard nodes**), first carpometacarpal joint, knees, hips.
- **Psoriatic arthritis:** DIP involvement, **dactylitis** ("sausage digit"), nail pitting and onycholysis, enthesitis; can be asymmetric oligoarthritis.
- **Axial spondyloarthritis:** inflammatory back pain beginning before about age 45, improving with exercise and not with rest, night pain, buttock pain from **sacroiliitis**, often **HLA-B27** positive, with uveitis.
- **Reactive arthritis:** asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis after gut or genitourinary infection.

**Synovial fluid analysis** is the key test for an effusion:
- Non-inflammatory (e.g. osteoarthritis): white cells below about 2,000 per µL.
- Inflammatory (e.g. RA, gout): about 2,000 to 50,000 per µL.
- Septic range: often above 50,000 per µL, neutrophil predominant, though overlap occurs.
- Always send Gram stain, culture and **polarized microscopy** for crystals.

**Blood tests** support but do not make the diagnosis: CRP and ESR, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, ANA, urate, HLA-B27. Ordering ANA or RF without clinical suspicion generates false positives, since low-titer ANA is common in healthy people.

**Imaging:** X-rays show joint space narrowing, osteophytes, erosions and chondrocalcinosis; ultrasound detects synovitis and effusions; MRI detects early sacroiliitis.

Red flags in joint and back pain include fever, weight loss, night sweats, history of cancer and neurological deficit.
levels.phd:
The inflammatory-versus-mechanical dichotomy maps onto distinct tissue biology. **Osteoarthritis** was long called non-inflammatory, but it is a whole-joint disease: chondrocytes shift toward a catabolic phenotype, releasing matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-13) and aggrecanases (ADAMTS-4 and -5) that degrade type II collagen and aggrecan; subchondral bone remodels and sclerosis appears; low-grade synovitis, driven partly by cartilage fragments acting as damage signals, contributes to pain. Pain correlates poorly with radiographic severity, partly because cartilage is aneural; pain arises from synovium, subchondral bone marrow lesions and central sensitization.

In **inflammatory synovitis**, the synovial lining expands into a pannus. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes become invasive and resist apoptosis, while macrophages and lymphocytes produce TNF, IL-6 and RANKL, activating osteoclasts that erode bone at the "bare areas" where synovium contacts bone uncovered by cartilage.

The **enthesis** is central to spondyloarthritis. The entheseal hypothesis proposes that mechanical stress at tendon and ligament insertions triggers IL-23-driven inflammation in resident immune cells, with IL-17 effector pathways, explaining enthesitis, dactylitis and new bone formation (syndesmophytes) in ankylosing spondylitis. HLA-B27's role remains debated: misfolding with an unfolded protein response, formation of heavy-chain homodimers recognized by killer cell receptors, and presentation of arthritogenic peptides are competing models. The gut-joint axis links spondyloarthritis with subclinical gut inflammation and inflammatory bowel disease.

Diagnostic reasoning benefits from **Bayesian thinking**: a positive ANA in a patient with only fatigue has a low positive predictive value for lupus, whereas the same result with photosensitive rash, nephritis and cytopenias is highly informative. Classification criteria (ACR/EULAR) are designed for research cohorts, not for diagnosing an individual patient, a distinction often misunderstood.
levels.expert:
A rheumatology attending reaches a diagnosis mostly by history and examination; tests confirm.

**First question: is this joint, or near the joint?** Bursitis, tendinopathy, enthesitis and referred pain (hip pain felt in the knee, especially in children with slipped capital femoral epiphysis) mimic arthritis. True synovitis causes pain throughout the range of motion and boggy swelling along the joint line.

**The acute hot joint:** aspirate before antibiotics whenever possible. Crystals do not exclude infection, since gout and sepsis can coexist. Prosthetic joints need orthopedic involvement before aspiration in many centers. In children, a limping febrile child needs septic arthritis and osteomyelitis excluded.

**Pattern recognition shortcuts:**
- Young adult with inflammatory back pain, heel pain and a red eye: spondyloarthritis.
- Older adult with new shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, high ESR and dramatic response to steroids: polymyalgia rheumatica; ask about headache, jaw claudication and visual symptoms to screen for **giant cell arteritis**, which can cause sudden blindness.
- Symmetric small-joint polyarthritis for more than six weeks: rheumatoid arthritis until proven otherwise. A self-limiting polyarthritis of a few weeks suggests a virus such as parvovirus B19.

**Neurological red flags:** back or neck pain with weakness, numbness, bladder or bowel changes, or saddle anesthesia suggests cord or cauda equina compression, a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent MRI. In rheumatoid arthritis, neck pain with neurological signs suggests **atlantoaxial instability**.

**Pitfalls:**
- Labeling everything in older adults as osteoarthritis and missing gout, pseudogout, infection or myeloma.
- Ordering autoimmune panels for fatigue and aches, then chasing a weakly positive ANA.
- Forgetting that the hip often refers pain to the knee.

keyPoints: Inflammatory pain: long morning stiffness, improves with use; mechanical: worse with use
Count joints: mono, oligo (2–4), poly (5 or more)
RA spares DIPs; OA has Heberden (DIP) and Bouchard (PIP) nodes; psoriatic arthritis involves DIPs and dactylitis
A single hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise: aspirate
Synovial fluid: cell count, Gram stain, culture and polarized microscopy
Back pain with saddle anesthesia or bladder change: urgent MRI for cauda equina

lessons.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Lupus

levels.kid:
Your immune system is like a team of guards that fights germs. Sometimes the guards get confused and attack your own body. That is called an **autoimmune** disease.

In **rheumatoid arthritis**, the guards attack the lining of the joints, especially in the hands and wrists. The joints get puffy, stiff and sore, often on both sides of the body.

In **lupus**, the guards can attack many places: skin, joints, kidneys, blood and more. Some people get a red rash across their cheeks and nose shaped like a butterfly.

Doctors cannot make these diseases disappear, but medicines can calm the guards down so people can live full, active lives.
levels.hs:
**Autoimmune diseases** happen when the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. Two important examples are rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.

**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)**
- Inflammation of the joint lining (synovium), usually in the **small joints of the hands and feet on both sides**: knuckles, middle finger joints and wrists.
- Morning stiffness lasting over an hour, swelling and tiredness.
- Without treatment, inflammation **erodes bone**, causing deformities such as fingers drifting toward the little finger.
- Blood tests: **rheumatoid factor** and **anti-CCP antibodies** (anti-CCP is more specific).
- Treatment started early with disease-modifying drugs such as **methotrexate**, and newer **biologic** drugs, can prevent joint damage.

**Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)**
- Much more common in women (about nine to one), often starting between the teens and forties.
- Can affect almost any organ: a **butterfly (malar) rash** over the cheeks that spares the folds beside the nose, rashes in sunlight, mouth ulcers, joint pain, inflammation around the heart and lungs, **kidney disease**, low blood counts and brain involvement.
- Blood tests: **ANA** is positive in nearly all patients but also in many healthy people; **anti-double-stranded DNA** and **anti-Smith** antibodies are more specific.
- **Hydroxychloroquine** is the backbone treatment for most patients.

Both diseases come in flares and quieter periods.
levels.college:
**Rheumatoid arthritis** affects about 0.5 to 1% of adults. Risk factors include HLA-DRB1 "shared epitope" alleles and **smoking**, which promotes citrullination of proteins in the lung; antibodies to citrullinated peptides (**anti-CCP**, specificity around 95%) can appear years before arthritis.

Features: symmetric polyarthritis of MCPs, PIPs, wrists and MTPs; **ulnar deviation**, **swan-neck** and **boutonnière** deformities, Z-thumb; rheumatoid nodules. Extra-articular disease includes interstitial lung disease, pleural effusion, scleritis, vasculitis, **Felty syndrome** (RA, splenomegaly and neutropenia), amyloidosis and accelerated cardiovascular disease. Cervical spine involvement can cause **atlantoaxial subluxation**.

Management is **treat-to-target**: start a conventional DMARD (methotrexate is the anchor) early, with short-term steroid bridging if needed, and escalate to biologics (TNF inhibitors, abatacept, tocilizumab, rituximab) or JAK inhibitors if remission or low disease activity is not reached. Screen for **latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B** before biologics.

**SLE** is a prototypic immune-complex disease. The 2019 EULAR/ACR classification requires an **ANA at a titer of at least 1:80** as an entry criterion, then weighted clinical and immunological domains. **Anti-dsDNA** levels and **low complement (C3, C4)** track activity, especially lupus nephritis, which is diagnosed by kidney biopsy and classified into ISN/RPS classes I to VI. Arthritis in lupus is typically non-erosive (Jaccoud arthropathy is deforming but reducible).

Related conditions: **drug-induced lupus** (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid; anti-histone antibodies; usually spares kidneys and brain), **antiphospholipid syndrome** (clots and pregnancy loss), and **neonatal lupus** from maternal anti-Ro antibodies, which can cause congenital heart block.

Hydroxychloroquine reduces flares and improves survival; regular **retinal screening** monitors for toxicity.
levels.phd:
Both diseases illustrate how loss of tolerance unfolds over years before symptoms.

**RA** progresses through a preclinical phase: genetic risk (the HLA-DRB1 shared epitope binds citrullinated peptides with high affinity) meets environmental triggers at mucosal sites (smoking in the lung, periodontal disease with Porphyromonas gingivalis, whose enzyme PPAD citrullinates proteins). Anti-citrullinated protein antibodies undergo epitope spreading and glycosylation changes before arthritis begins. In the synovium, fibroblast-like synoviocytes become effector cells with an aggressive, invasive phenotype; single-cell studies have identified distinct fibroblast subsets for tissue destruction versus inflammation. The success of TNF blockade, IL-6 receptor blockade, B-cell depletion with rituximab, T-cell costimulation blockade with abatacept and JAK inhibition shows that several pathways can be targeted, yet about a third of patients respond inadequately to any single agent, reflecting molecular heterogeneity (lympho-myeloid, diffuse-myeloid and pauci-immune fibroid synovial pathotypes).

**SLE** centers on defective clearance of apoptotic debris and nuclear antigens. Inherited deficiency of early complement components (C1q, C4, C2) confers a very high lupus risk, supporting the waste disposal hypothesis. Immune complexes containing nucleic acids activate plasmacytoid dendritic cells via TLR7 and TLR9, producing **type I interferon**; an **interferon signature** is present in most patients. TLR7 gene dosage helps explain female predominance, since TLR7 can escape X-inactivation; a gain-of-function TLR7 variant has been described as a monogenic cause. These insights led to anifrolumab (type I interferon receptor antibody) and belimumab (anti-BAFF). Experimental CD19 CAR-T therapy has produced drug-free remissions in small cohorts of refractory lupus, suggesting that resetting the B-cell compartment can restore tolerance.
levels.expert:
**Rheumatoid arthritis in practice:**
- The window of opportunity is early: synovitis treated within the first few months responds better and erodes less. Refer patients with persistent synovitis promptly; do not wait for positive serology, since about a fifth to a third are seronegative.
- Monitor methotrexate with blood counts and liver function tests; folic acid supplementation reduces side effects; it is teratogenic and must be stopped well before conception.
- Infection risk with biologics is real: screen for latent TB, hepatitis B and C, update vaccines, and teach patients to seek care early with fever.
- Cardiovascular risk is roughly comparable to diabetes; manage blood pressure, lipids and smoking aggressively.

**The neurosurgical and anesthetic angle:** long-standing RA can cause **atlantoaxial subluxation**. Before intubation or neck manipulation, ask about neck pain, occipital headache and limb paresthesias, and get flexion-extension imaging when indicated. Cervical myelopathy from RA may need surgical stabilization.

**Lupus in practice:**
- Lupus is a great mimic, and a positive ANA alone does not make the diagnosis; build the case from organ involvement and specific antibodies.
- Check urine at every visit: protein and casts are the earliest signs of nephritis, which is often silent.
- In a lupus patient with fever, think infection first (immunosuppression) before attributing it to a flare; low complement and rising anti-dsDNA favor a flare.
- **Neuropsychiatric lupus** includes seizures, psychosis, stroke and cognitive dysfunction; antiphospholipid antibodies, infection and drug effects must be excluded.
- Pregnancy planning: disease should be quiet for months before conception; hydroxychloroquine is continued; anti-Ro positive mothers need fetal heart monitoring.
- Steroids control flares quickly but cause much of the long-term damage (osteoporosis, avascular necrosis, diabetes, infection); the goal is the lowest exposure possible.

keyPoints: RA: symmetric small-joint polyarthritis (MCP, PIP, wrist), sparing DIPs; anti-CCP is highly specific
RA treatment: early DMARD (methotrexate), treat-to-target, biologics; screen for TB and hepatitis B first
RA can cause atlantoaxial subluxation: important before intubation and neck surgery
SLE: malar rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, serositis, nephritis, cytopenias, neuropsychiatric disease
ANA is sensitive; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific; low C3/C4 and high anti-dsDNA track flares
Hydroxychloroquine is the backbone of lupus therapy

lessons.title: Gout and Septic Arthritis

levels.kid:
Sometimes a joint suddenly becomes very red, hot, puffy and so sore that even a bed sheet touching it hurts. Two big reasons are **gout** and **germs**.

**Gout** happens when a waste chemical called **uric acid** builds up in the blood and forms tiny, sharp, needle-like crystals in a joint. It often starts in the big toe, usually at night.

**Septic arthritis** is when germs get inside a joint. It can damage the joint very fast, so it is an emergency.

To tell them apart, a doctor uses a needle to take a little fluid out of the joint and looks at it under a microscope. Then they know which treatment is right.
levels.hs:
**Gout** is the most common inflammatory arthritis in adults. It happens when **uric acid**, made when the body breaks down purines, builds up and forms **monosodium urate crystals** in joints.

A classic gout attack:
- Starts suddenly, often overnight
- Usually affects **one joint**, most often the **base of the big toe** (called podagra)
- The joint becomes red, hot, swollen and extremely tender
- Triggers include alcohol (especially beer), large meals of red meat or seafood, sugary drinks, dehydration, surgery and some water pills (diuretics)

Over years, untreated gout can cause **tophi**, chalky lumps of crystals under the skin, and kidney stones. Attacks are treated with anti-inflammatory medicines, colchicine or steroids. Long-term, drugs such as **allopurinol** lower uric acid to dissolve crystals.

**Pseudogout** is a similar attack caused by **calcium pyrophosphate** crystals, often in the knee of an older person.

**Septic arthritis** is a bacterial infection inside a joint, most commonly caused by **Staphylococcus aureus**. Fever, a hot swollen joint and refusing to move it are typical. Bacteria can destroy cartilage within days. Treatment is draining the joint (by needle or surgery) and antibiotics.

The crucial step for any hot joint is **joint aspiration**: fluid is tested for crystals, cells and bacteria. Gout and infection can even happen together.
levels.college:
**Crystal identification under polarized light:**
- **Monosodium urate (gout):** needle-shaped, **strongly negatively birefringent** (yellow when aligned parallel to the compensator axis).
- **Calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD, pseudogout):** rhomboid or rod-shaped, **weakly positively birefringent** (blue when parallel). X-rays may show **chondrocalcinosis**.

**Gout essentials:** hyperuricemia arises mostly from **underexcretion** by the kidney, less often overproduction (tumor lysis, myeloproliferative disease). Serum urate can be **normal during an acute flare**, so a normal level does not exclude gout. Dual-energy CT can detect urate deposits.

Acute flare treatment: NSAIDs, colchicine or corticosteroids (oral or intra-articular once infection is excluded), chosen around kidney function and comorbidities. **Urate-lowering therapy (ULT)** is indicated for recurrent flares, tophi, radiographic damage or urate kidney stones. Xanthine oxidase inhibitors (**allopurinol**, febuxostat) are first line, titrated to a target serum urate below about **0.36 mmol/L** (lower for tophaceous disease). Flare prophylaxis is used when starting ULT, because rapid urate shifts can trigger flares. Patients already on ULT should **continue it during a flare**. Screening for **HLA-B\*58:01** before allopurinol is recommended in higher-risk ancestries (for example Han Chinese, Korean, Thai and African American patients) because of the risk of severe cutaneous reactions.

**Septic arthritis:**
- Organisms: **S. aureus** most commonly; streptococci; **Neisseria gonorrhoeae** in sexually active young adults (often with tenosynovitis and pustules); gram-negatives in older or immunocompromised patients; **Kingella kingae** in young children.
- Risk factors: existing joint disease (RA), prosthetic joints, diabetes, immunosuppression, skin infection, recent joint injection.
- Management: aspirate before antibiotics, empirical IV therapy guided by Gram stain, and joint drainage by repeated aspiration, arthroscopic or open washout.
levels.phd:
Humans have high serum urate because of evolutionary loss of **uricase** in hominoid ancestors during the Miocene, through serial mutations. Hypotheses for this include urate's antioxidant capacity and a role in maintaining blood pressure on low-salt diets, as well as enhanced fructose-driven fat storage during food scarcity. About two thirds of urate is excreted by the kidney, where **URAT1** (SLC22A12) and **GLUT9** (SLC2A9) reabsorb it, and **ABCG2** secretes it in gut and kidney; GWAS variants in these transporters explain much heritable gout risk, and the ABCG2 Q141K variant impairs excretion.

Crystals alone do not cause inflammation; many hyperuricemic people never develop gout, and urate deposits can be clinically silent. Flares begin when crystals are phagocytosed by resident macrophages and activate the **NLRP3 inflammasome**, cleaving pro-IL-1β to active **IL-1β**, which recruits neutrophils. A second signal, such as free fatty acids or TLR ligands, primes the response, explaining links to large meals and alcohol. Flares resolve partly through **aggregated neutrophil extracellular traps** that trap crystals and degrade cytokines. Colchicine disrupts microtubules, impairing neutrophil migration and inflammasome assembly; IL-1 blockers such as canakinumab and anakinra work in refractory flares.

In **septic arthritis**, cartilage destruction begins within hours to days: bacterial proteases, host matrix metalloproteinases from neutrophils and synoviocytes, and raised intra-articular pressure that reduces blood supply all contribute. S. aureus expresses adhesins (MSCRAMMs) such as collagen-binding protein that anchor it to cartilage, and it can invade and survive within osteoblasts and synoviocytes, sheltering from antibiotics. Prosthetic joint infection involves biofilm, which is why debridement with implant retention often fails if symptoms have lasted more than a few weeks and why staged revision surgery is common.
levels.expert:
**The approach to the acute hot joint:** aspirate, then decide. A clinician who treats a presumed gout flare without aspirating will eventually miss a septic joint.

**Aspiration pearls:**
- Send cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture (in blood culture bottles to increase yield) and crystal microscopy.
- A negative Gram stain does not exclude infection; culture is positive in most non-gonococcal cases, but gonococcal joint cultures are often negative, so test urethral, cervical, rectal and throat sites with nucleic acid tests.
- Blood cultures are positive in a substantial minority.
- Never inject steroid into a joint until infection is excluded.

**Gout pitfalls:**
- A normal urate during a flare. Recheck two weeks later.
- Diuretics are a common driver; consider switching where appropriate, since losartan has a mild uric acid-lowering effect.
- **Treat to target**: many patients stay on a starting allopurinol amount forever with ongoing flares. Titrate to the urate goal, monitor kidney function, and explain the plan: ULT is long-term, flares may increase early, and lifestyle changes help but rarely suffice alone.
- Check for comorbidities: hypertension, kidney disease, metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease cluster with gout.

**Septic arthritis pitfalls:**
- Older patients and those on steroids or biologics may have little fever.
- In children with a hot hip, the **Kocher criteria** (non-weight-bearing, fever, raised ESR and white count) help separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis; ultrasound-guided aspiration confirms.
- **Prosthetic joint pain** with a sinus tract is infection until proven otherwise; involve orthopedics early and avoid antibiotics before aspiration if the patient is stable.
- Septic arthritis of the sternoclavicular or sacroiliac joint suggests bacteremia, often from endocarditis or an infected intravenous line.

keyPoints: Gout: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals; podagra (first MTP)
Pseudogout (CPPD): rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals; chondrocalcinosis
Serum urate can be normal during a flare
Urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol) treated to target; continue it during flares
Septic arthritis: S. aureus most common; aspirate before antibiotics; drain the joint
Crystals do not exclude infection

lessons.title: Describing Skin Lesions

levels.kid:
Skin doctors are like detectives who use special words to describe what they see. That way, any doctor reading the notes can picture the spot.

A flat spot you can see but not feel is a **macule**, like a freckle. A small bump you can feel is a **papule**, like a mosquito bite. A blister with clear fluid is a **vesicle**. A bump with yellow pus is a **pustule**.

Doctors also look at the color, the size, the shape, and where the spots are on the body.

One cool trick: they press a clear glass on a red spot. If the red fades, blood is just flowing under the skin. If it does not fade, blood has leaked out, and that needs a doctor quickly.
levels.hs:
Dermatology has its own vocabulary so that a lesion can be described precisely. **Primary lesions** are the first changes caused by a disease:
- **Macule:** flat, color change, under about 1 cm (a freckle). A larger flat area is a **patch**.
- **Papule:** raised, solid, under about 1 cm. A larger, flat-topped raised area is a **plaque** (psoriasis).
- **Nodule:** a deeper, solid lump, usually over 1 cm.
- **Vesicle:** a small fluid-filled blister; a large one is a **bulla**.
- **Pustule:** a blister filled with pus (acne).
- **Wheal:** a raised, itchy, short-lived swelling (hives).

**Secondary changes** develop over time or from scratching: **scale** (flaky skin), **crust** (dried fluid), **erosion** (loss of the top layer), **ulcer** (deeper loss), **excoriation** (scratch marks), **lichenification** (thickened skin from rubbing) and **scar**.

Doctors also describe:
- **Color:** red, brown, violet, white, yellow
- **Shape and arrangement:** round, ring-shaped (annular), lines (linear), clusters, along a nerve band (dermatomal, like shingles)
- **Distribution:** sun-exposed areas, elbows and knees, skin folds, one side of the body

**Blanching:** pressing a glass on a red lesion. **Petechiae** (pinpoint spots) and **purpura** (larger spots) do not blanch because blood has left the vessels. A non-blanching rash with fever can mean meningococcal infection.

Redness looks different on darker skin, often brown, purple or gray, so doctors must learn to recognize disease on all skin tones.
levels.college:
A complete lesion description follows a sequence: **site and distribution**, **number**, **size**, **color**, **morphology** (primary lesion), **configuration**, **surface** (secondary features) and **palpation**. For example: "multiple well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on the extensor elbows and knees" is psoriasis described in one sentence.

Size thresholds differ between sources (0.5 cm or 1 cm separate macule from patch and papule from plaque); be consistent and measure.

**Configuration terms:** annular (tinea corporis, granuloma annulare), targetoid (**erythema multiforme**, with three concentric zones), linear (contact with plants, Koebner phenomenon), grouped or herpetiform (herpes simplex), dermatomal (herpes zoster), reticular or net-like (livedo reticularis), serpiginous (cutaneous larva migrans).

**Distribution clues:**
- Extensor surfaces: psoriasis.
- Flexures (inside elbows and knees): atopic eczema in older children and adults.
- Sun-exposed areas: photosensitive eruptions, lupus, drug reactions.
- Palms and soles: secondary syphilis, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, erythema multiforme.

**Bedside signs:**
- **Diascopy** (glass pressure) separates erythema from purpura.
- **Nikolsky sign:** gentle lateral pressure shears the epidermis; positive in pemphigus vulgaris, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and SJS/TEN.
- **Koebner phenomenon:** lesions appearing in sites of trauma (psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo).
- **Auspitz sign:** pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scale is removed.
- **Darier sign:** a wheal after stroking a mastocytoma.

**Tools:** dermoscopy magnifies pigment patterns, Wood's lamp shows fluorescence of some fungi and pigment changes, KOH preparation detects fungi, and biopsy (punch, shave or excision) provides histology and immunofluorescence.
levels.phd:
Morphology maps onto skin histology. A **macule** reflects a change in pigment or vascularity without thickening; a **papule or plaque** reflects epidermal hyperplasia (psoriasis: acanthosis with parakeratosis), dermal infiltrate or deposition. **Scale** indicates abnormal keratinization: parakeratosis (retained nuclei in the stratum corneum) produces silvery psoriatic scale, whereas orthokeratotic scale is seen in ichthyoses. **Lichenification** reflects chronic rubbing, with thickened epidermis and accentuated skin lines.

**Blister level** has diagnostic power. Intraepidermal blisters are flaccid and rupture easily: in **pemphigus vulgaris**, autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (and 1 in mucocutaneous disease) disrupt desmosomes, producing acantholysis just above the basal layer and a positive Nikolsky sign. Direct immunofluorescence shows a "fishnet" intercellular IgG pattern. In **bullous pemphigoid**, antibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230 split the dermal-epidermal junction, giving tense blisters with linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane. The **desmoglein compensation hypothesis** explains distribution: desmoglein 1 dominates superficial epidermis, desmoglein 3 the deeper layers and mucosa, so antibody profile predicts where blisters form. The same logic explains why staphylococcal exfoliative toxin, which cleaves desmoglein 1, causes superficial peeling.

**Blaschko lines** are invisible developmental lines along which mosaic skin disorders (incontinentia pigmenti, linear epidermal nevi) follow, representing migration paths of embryonic clones, distinct from dermatomes (sensory nerve territories) and Langer lines (tension lines).

Diagnostic inequity is a research focus: textbook images historically underrepresented skin of color, and studies have found clinicians identify conditions less accurately on darker skin, which contributes to delayed diagnosis of melanoma, Kawasaki disease and cyanosis. Pulse oximeter overestimation of oxygen saturation in darker skin is a related measurement bias.
levels.expert:
Experienced dermatologists describe first and diagnose second; a precise description produces a short differential.

**Practical habits:**
- Examine the whole skin in good light, including scalp, nails, mouth, genitals, palms and soles. The diagnosis is often in a place the patient did not mention.
- Touch the lesion: is it soft, firm, fixed, warm, tender? Is the scale fine or thick?
- Find a primary lesion; scratched, crusted or treated skin hides the original morphology.
- Ask about timing, itch, pain, new medicines, exposures and systemic symptoms.

**Emergencies hidden in rashes:**
- **Non-blanching rash with fever:** meningococcal disease until proven otherwise; antibiotics immediately.
- **Painful skin, mucosal erosions and positive Nikolsky sign after a new drug:** Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Stop the culprit (commonly allopurinol, certain antiepileptics, sulfonamides, nevirapine) and refer to a burns or intensive care unit.
- **Fever, widespread rash, facial swelling, eosinophilia and organ involvement weeks after starting a drug:** DRESS.
- **Erythroderma** (red skin over most of the body): risk of fluid loss, hypothermia and high-output heart failure.
- **Palpable purpura:** small-vessel vasculitis; check urine for kidney involvement.

**Skin of color:**
- Erythema can appear violaceous, dark brown or gray; assess warmth, swelling and texture instead of relying on redness.
- Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is common and distressing; treat inflammation early.
- Acral and nail melanoma, and keloids, deserve special attention.

**Documentation:** write the description, measure the lesion, and photograph it with consent. "Rash on arm" is useless to the next clinician; "a 3 cm annular plaque with a scaly raised edge and central clearing on the left forearm" suggests tinea immediately.

keyPoints: Flat: macule (small) and patch (large); raised: papule (small) and plaque (large); deep: nodule
Fluid: vesicle (small) and bulla (large); pus: pustule; transient swelling: wheal
Secondary changes: scale, crust, erosion, ulcer, excoriation, lichenification, scar
Describe site, distribution, number, size, color, shape, configuration and surface
Non-blanching petechiae or purpura with fever can mean meningococcal disease
Pemphigus: flaccid blisters, Nikolsky positive; pemphigoid: tense blisters

lessons.title: Skin Cancer

levels.kid:
The sun gives us light and warmth, but its invisible **UV rays** can hurt the cells in our skin. Over many years, too much sun can make some skin cells grow when they should not. That is skin cancer.

Most skin cancers grow slowly and can be removed by a doctor. One kind, called **melanoma**, can be more dangerous, so it is important to find it early.

Doctors teach a trick to check moles called **ABCDE**: is the mole lopsided, does it have a messy edge, many colors, is it big, or is it changing?

You can protect your skin with sunscreen, hats, shade and by never getting sunburned on purpose.
levels.hs:
Skin cancer is the most common cancer in many countries. The main cause is **ultraviolet (UV) radiation** from the sun and tanning beds, which damages DNA in skin cells. Fair skin, many moles, severe sunburns in childhood, a family history and a weakened immune system raise the risk.

There are three main types:
- **Basal cell carcinoma (BCC):** the most common. A pearly, shiny bump, often with tiny visible blood vessels, on sun-exposed skin like the face. It grows slowly and very rarely spreads, but can damage nearby tissue if ignored.
- **Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC):** a scaly, crusted or bleeding bump, often on the face, ears, lips or hands. It can spread if not treated. It often starts from rough, scaly sun spots called **actinic keratoses**.
- **Melanoma:** cancer of the **melanocytes**, the pigment cells. Less common but responsible for most skin cancer deaths because it can spread to the lymph nodes, lungs, liver and brain.

The **ABCDE** rule helps spot melanoma:
- **A**symmetry
- **B**order irregularity
- **C**olor variation
- **D**iameter over about 6 mm
- **E**volving (changing size, shape or color)

A mole that looks different from all the others, the **"ugly duckling,"** is also suspicious.

Melanoma found early is usually cured by surgery. Prevention is simple: sunscreen, protective clothing, shade, and avoiding tanning beds.
levels.college:
**Basal cell carcinoma** arises from basal keratinocytes and is driven by **Hedgehog pathway** activation, usually loss of **PTCH1** or activating **SMO** mutations (Gorlin syndrome is germline PTCH1). Subtypes include nodular (pearly with telangiectasia and rolled edges, ulcerating as a "rodent ulcer"), superficial (a scaly pink patch) and morpheaform (scar-like, aggressive). Metastasis is very rare. Treatment is excision, **Mohs micrographic surgery** for high-risk facial sites, or topical therapy and curettage for superficial lesions; Hedgehog inhibitors (vismodegib) treat advanced disease.

**Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma** frequently carries UV-signature **TP53** mutations (C-to-T transitions at dipyrimidine sites). Precursors are actinic keratoses and **Bowen disease** (SCC in situ). Risk is greatly increased in **organ transplant recipients** on immunosuppression. High-risk features include lip and ear location, size, depth, poor differentiation and **perineural invasion**, which can track along cranial nerves.

**Melanoma** subtypes: superficial spreading (most common in fair-skinned people), nodular (vertical growth from the start, so ABCD may not apply; "EFG": elevated, firm, growing), lentigo maligna (chronically sun-damaged face of older adults) and **acral lentiginous** (palms, soles, nail beds; the most common subtype in people with darker skin, not linked to UV). **Hutchinson sign** is pigment spreading from the nail onto the nail fold.

Prognosis of a primary melanoma depends most on **Breslow thickness** (depth in millimeters), plus ulceration and mitotic rate. Staging uses **sentinel lymph node biopsy** for thicker lesions. About half of cutaneous melanomas carry **BRAF V600** mutations; others carry NRAS, NF1 or KIT mutations.

Advanced melanoma treatment was transformed by **immune checkpoint inhibitors** (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4) and **BRAF plus MEK inhibitors**.
levels.phd:
Ultraviolet B is absorbed directly by DNA, forming **cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers** and 6-4 photoproducts, repaired by nucleotide excision repair; inherited defects in this pathway (xeroderma pigmentosum) raise skin cancer risk roughly a thousand-fold and cause cancers in childhood. UVA penetrates deeper and acts mainly through reactive oxygen species. Melanoma has one of the highest tumor mutational burdens of any cancer, dominated by the UV signature, which helps explain its unusual responsiveness to immunotherapy: more mutations mean more neoantigens visible to T cells.

Melanoma evolution often proceeds stepwise: BRAF V600E is found even in benign nevi, where it triggers **oncogene-induced senescence**; progression requires further hits such as TERT promoter mutations (creating new transcription factor binding sites), CDKN2A loss (removing p16 and the senescence brake), and PTEN or TP53 alterations. Germline CDKN2A mutations account for many familial melanoma kindreds.

Targeted therapy illustrates **pathway reactivation**: BRAF inhibitors alone cause rapid responses but resistance arises through MAPK pathway reactivation (NRAS mutation, BRAF splice variants, MEK mutation). Paradoxically, BRAF inhibitors activate MAPK signaling in BRAF wild-type cells via RAF dimerization, causing cutaneous SCCs; adding MEK inhibitors reduces both resistance and this paradoxical effect.

Checkpoint immunotherapy changed survival dramatically. Before 2011, median survival for metastatic melanoma was under a year; with combined anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 therapy, long-term follow-up from CheckMate 067 shows more than 40% of patients alive at ten years. Immune-related adverse events (colitis, hepatitis, hypophysitis, thyroiditis, myocarditis) reflect loss of peripheral tolerance. Neoadjuvant immunotherapy before surgery for resectable stage III disease improved event-free survival over adjuvant therapy in recent trials, suggesting the intact tumor primes a stronger T-cell response.
levels.expert:
**Skin checks done well:**
- Examine the whole skin, including scalp, soles, between toes, nails and genitals. Acral and nail melanomas are missed because nobody looked.
- Use the **ugly duckling** sign and dermoscopy; serial photography helps people with many moles.
- Ask about change: a new or changing lesion in an adult, especially over age 40, deserves suspicion.
- **Amelanotic melanoma** is pink or red and does not look pigmented; nodular melanoma grows fast and may not fit ABCD.

**Biopsy principles:** a suspected melanoma is ideally **excised whole** with a narrow margin so the pathologist can measure Breslow thickness accurately; shave biopsies that transect the lesion can understage it. Wide local excision margins and sentinel node biopsy follow the pathology.

**Neurosurgical relevance:** melanoma is one of the cancers most likely to spread to the **brain**, along with lung, breast and kidney cancer. Melanoma brain metastases are often multiple and hemorrhagic. Management combines stereotactic radiosurgery, surgical resection for large symptomatic lesions, and immunotherapy, which has meaningful intracranial response rates. A patient with a history of melanoma and new headaches, seizures or focal signs needs urgent brain imaging, even many years after the primary.

**SCC with perineural invasion** can travel along the trigeminal or facial nerves toward the skull base; facial numbness, tingling or weakness in a patient with a past head and neck SCC needs MRI.

**Transplant recipients** develop many aggressive SCCs; regular skin surveillance and adjusting immunosuppression are part of care.

**Prevention advice that works:** daily broad-spectrum sunscreen on exposed skin (a randomized Australian trial showed reduced melanoma), protective clothing, shade in the middle of the day and no tanning beds. Skin of color still develops skin cancer, often diagnosed later.

keyPoints: UV radiation causes DNA damage (pyrimidine dimers); tanning beds increase risk
BCC: most common, pearly with telangiectasia, Hedgehog pathway, rarely metastasizes
SCC: from actinic keratoses, TP53 mutations, higher risk in transplant recipients, perineural spread
Melanoma ABCDE: asymmetry, border, color, diameter over about 6 mm, evolving; ugly duckling sign
Breslow thickness is the key prognostic factor; about half carry BRAF V600
Melanoma commonly spreads to the brain; immunotherapy transformed survival
